questions.x: The route table, not the subnet itself, decides the type. An internet gateway route makes a subnet public; outbound-only access through NAT keeps it private.

questions.t: AWS suggests Transit Gateway for self-managed routing between many VPCs, and AWS Cloud WAN when you want AWS to manage a global WAN with central policy.
questions.f: AWS suggests Cloud WAN for self-managed routing between many VPCs, and AWS Transit Gateway when you want AWS to manage a global WAN with central policy.
questions.x: Transit Gateway is a hub you configure and route yourself, including across Regions. Cloud WAN is the managed wide-area network option driven by a central policy, so the false statement swaps their roles.

questions.t: AWS points to Global Accelerator for latency-sensitive applications such as gaming, IoT and VoIP, and to CloudFront for cutting latency on web content.
questions.f: AWS points to CloudFront for latency-sensitive applications such as gaming, IoT and VoIP, and to Global Accelerator for cutting latency on web content.
questions.x: CloudFront is the CDN that caches and delivers web content from the edge. Global Accelerator gives static IPs and carries traffic over the AWS network to the nearest healthy endpoint, which suits non-cacheable, latency-sensitive traffic.

questions.t: For workloads leaving AWS App Mesh, AWS recommends Amazon VPC Lattice on Amazon EKS and Amazon ECS Service Connect on Amazon ECS.
questions.f: For workloads leaving AWS App Mesh, AWS recommends Amazon ECS Service Connect on Amazon EKS and Amazon VPC Lattice on Amazon ECS.
questions.x: App Mesh closed to new customers in September 2024 and was set to be discontinued on 2026-09-30. Service Connect is an ECS feature, so it cannot be the EKS answer; VPC Lattice is the recommended path for EKS.

questions.t: On AWS, the US East and US West Regions hold DoD Impact Level 2, while IL4 and IL5 workloads belong in AWS GovCloud (US) (as of 2026-11).
questions.f: On AWS, the US East and US West Regions hold DoD Impact Level 4, while IL5 and IL6 workloads belong in AWS GovCloud (US) (as of 2026-11).
questions.x: The commercial US Regions are authorized only at IL2. GovCloud (US) holds IL2, IL4 and IL5, and classified IL6 work goes to the AWS Secret Region instead.

questions.t: DoD impact levels 1 and 3 were folded into the next level up, which is why the levels in use are IL2, IL4, IL5 and IL6.
questions.f: DoD impact levels 3 and 5 were folded into the next level up, which is why the levels in use are IL1, IL2, IL4 and IL6.
questions.x: The scheme skips odd numbers at the low end because former levels 1 and 3 were merged upward. IL5 is very much in use for higher-sensitivity CUI and National Security Systems.

questions.t: Private connectivity for DoD IL4 and IL5 workloads runs through a DoD CIO-approved Cloud Access Point that the mission owner, not the cloud provider, connects to.
questions.f: Private connectivity for DoD IL4 and IL5 workloads runs through a DoD CIO-approved Cloud Access Point that the cloud provider, not the mission owner, connects to.
questions.x: Connecting to a Cloud Access Point is the mission owner's job under the SRG. It is one of several areas, along with OS and application STIGs, that stay with the customer rather than being inherited from AWS.

questions.t: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS secures the cloud itself, while customers secure what they run in it, such as their content, applications and networks.
questions.f: Under the shared responsibility model, customers secure the cloud itself, while AWS secures what they run in it, such as their content, applications and networks.
questions.x: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud, and the customer for security in the cloud. The AWS security services are tools for that customer half, which is why the false statement's split is backwards.

questions.t: The AWS SRA makes a Security Tooling account the delegated administrator for services like GuardDuty and Security Hub, and keeps organization CloudTrail logs in a Log Archive account.
questions.f: The AWS SRA makes a Log Archive account the delegated administrator for services like GuardDuty and Security Hub, and keeps organization CloudTrail logs in a Security Tooling account.
questions.x: In the reference architecture the Security Tooling account (Control Tower's Audit account) administers the detection services, while Log Archive stores CloudTrail logs and Config snapshots. Neither job is meant for the management account.

questions.t: Amazon Macie uses machine learning to discover sensitive data, while Amazon GuardDuty is the AWS service for threat detection.
questions.f: Amazon GuardDuty uses machine learning to discover sensitive data, while Amazon Macie is the AWS service for threat detection.
questions.x: The AWS SRA lists Macie under data protection for finding sensitive data, and GuardDuty under threat detection and continuous monitoring. The false statement swaps the two services.

questions.t: An EventBridge pipe connects one source to one target, while an EventBridge event bus routes events from many sources to many targets.
questions.f: An EventBridge event bus connects one source to one target, while an EventBridge pipe routes events from many sources to many targets.
questions.x: Pipes are point-to-point, with optional filtering and enrichment in between. Buses are routers that deliver each event to zero or more targets by rule, and the two are often combined.

questions.t: A rule on a classic EventBridge event bus can have at most 5 targets, and that quota is fixed.
questions.f: A rule on a classic EventBridge event bus can have at most 50 targets, and that quota is fixed.
questions.x: Classic buses allow 300 rules per bus by default (adjustable) but only 5 targets per rule, which cannot be raised. Wider fan-out needs more rules or another routing layer.

questions.t: By default, a classic EventBridge bus retries delivery to a target for 24 hours and up to 185 times.
questions.f: By default, a classic EventBridge bus retries delivery to a target for 2 hours and up to 18 times.
questions.x: EventBridge keeps retrying failed deliveries for a day and up to 185 attempts, but delivery is at-least-once and it does not persist events like a queue, so consumers should be idempotent.

questions.t: A Regional EFS file system stores data across several Availability Zones, while a One Zone file system keeps it in one AZ and can lose data if that AZ is damaged.
questions.f: A One Zone EFS file system stores data across several Availability Zones, while a Regional file system keeps it in one AZ and can lose data if that AZ is damaged.
questions.x: Regional is AWS's recommended type and stays available through AZ failures. One Zone trades that resilience for a single-AZ footprint, which is why AWS turns on backups by default for it.

questions.t: The default Amazon EFS lifecycle policy moves files to Infrequent Access after 30 days without access and to Archive after 90 days.
questions.f: The default Amazon EFS lifecycle policy moves files to Infrequent Access after 90 days without access and to Archive after 180 days.
questions.x: EFS tiers untouched files to IA at 30 days and to Archive at 90 days by default. Intelligent-Tiering can bring a file back to Standard when it is read again.

questions.t: Amazon EFS encryption at rest must be chosen when the file system is created, while encryption in transit is turned on when a client mounts it.
questions.f: Amazon EFS encryption in transit must be chosen when the file system is created, while encryption at rest is turned on when a client mounts it.
questions.x: At-rest encryption with AWS KMS is a creation-time setting of the file system. TLS for data in transit is enabled per mount, using the EFS mount helper, so the false statement swaps the two.

questions.t: Amazon Textract's DetectDocumentText API returns plain OCR text, while AnalyzeDocument also returns structure such as form key-value pairs and tables.
questions.f: Amazon Textract's AnalyzeDocument API returns plain OCR text, while DetectDocumentText also returns structure such as form key-value pairs and tables.
questions.x: DetectDocumentText is the basic OCR call. AnalyzeDocument adds forms, tables, signatures, layout and Queries so the output keeps the page's relationships, which is why the false statement has them reversed.

questions.t: By default, asynchronous Amazon Textract results sit in a Textract-owned bucket and can be retrieved for only 7 days after the job starts.
questions.f: By default, asynchronous Amazon Textract results sit in a Textract-owned bucket and can be retrieved for up to 90 days after the job starts.
questions.x: Textract keeps default async output for just 7 days. To keep results longer, set OutputConfig so they are written to your own S3 bucket, optionally encrypted with a customer managed KMS key.

questions.t: In AWS's US West (Oregon) example rates, Textract Forms costs $0.05 per page versus $0.0015 for DetectDocumentText text detection (as of 2026-11).
questions.f: In AWS's US West (Oregon) example rates, Textract Forms costs $0.0015 per page versus $0.05 for DetectDocumentText text detection (as of 2026-11).
questions.x: Each Textract feature is billed per page on its own, and Forms is far pricier than raw text detection for the first million pages. Requesting Forms when you only need text multiplies the cost by more than 30.

questions.t: In an Amazon EMR cluster, core nodes run tasks and store HDFS data, while task nodes only run tasks and hold no HDFS data.
questions.f: In an Amazon EMR cluster, task nodes run tasks and store HDFS data, while core nodes only run tasks and hold no HDFS data.
questions.x: Core nodes carry HDFS, so multi-node clusters need at least one. Task nodes are pure compute, which makes them optional and the safe place to add or remove capacity such as Spot.

questions.t: Data kept only in an Amazon EMR cluster's HDFS is lost when the cluster terminates, so durable input and output usually live in Amazon S3.
questions.f: Data kept only in an Amazon EMR cluster's HDFS is saved to Amazon S3 automatically when the cluster terminates, so it survives the cluster.
questions.x: HDFS on EMR is ephemeral and disappears with the cluster, even after a failure. Keeping durable data in S3 through EMRFS or S3A is what makes short-lived, job-scoped clusters practical.

questions.t: An Amazon EMR on EC2 cluster can run one or three primary nodes, and the three-node option needs EMR release 5.23.0 or later.
questions.f: An Amazon EMR on EC2 cluster can run one or two primary nodes, and the two-node option needs EMR release 5.23.0 or later.
questions.x: For primary-node high availability EMR supports three primary nodes, starting with release 5.23.0. There is no two-primary configuration.

questions.t: Security pillar best practice SEC01-BP01 calls for separating workloads and environments into different AWS accounts organized into OUs.
questions.f: Security pillar best practice SEC01-BP01 calls for separating workloads and environments into different VPCs inside one shared AWS account.
questions.x: SEC01-BP01 uses accounts as the isolation boundary, grouped into organizational units whose controls member accounts inherit. Mixing workloads of different data sensitivity in one account is one of its named anti-patterns.

questions.t: The Security pillar's apply-security-at-all-layers principle means defense in depth, from the network edge and VPC down to the application and its code.
questions.f: The Security pillar's maintain-traceability principle means defense in depth, from the network edge and VPC down to the application and its code.
questions.x: Layered controls are the point of applying security at all layers. Maintaining traceability is a different principle, about monitoring, alerting on and auditing actions in real time.

questions.t: The Security pillar's application security guidance puts threat modeling in the design phase, so flaws are caught while they are still cheap to fix.
questions.f: The Security pillar's application security guidance puts threat modeling after deployment, so flaws are judged against how the application really runs.
questions.x: SEC 11 covers security across design, development and deployment, and it places threat modeling early. Finding a design flaw before code is written costs far less than fixing it in production.

questions.t: The SAP-C02 Solutions Architect – Professional exam is pass/fail on a 100–1,000 scale, with a scaled score of 750 needed to pass.
questions.f: The SAP-C02 Solutions Architect – Professional exam is pass/fail on a 100–1,000 scale, with a scaled score of 720 needed to pass.
questions.x: The SAP-C02 exam guide sets the passing mark at 750, under a compensatory model where only the overall score counts. 720 is not the Professional exam's threshold.

questions.t: SAP-C03 took over Solutions Architect – Professional exam delivery on November 17, 2026, the day after the last SAP-C02 sitting.
questions.f: SAP-C03 takes over Solutions Architect – Professional exam delivery on December 1, 2026, the day after the last SAP-C02 sitting.
questions.x: AWS set November 16, 2026 as the final day for SAP-C02 and began SAP-C03 delivery on November 17. Credentials earned on SAP-C02 stay valid until their original expiry.

questions.t: The AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional exam gives candidates 180 minutes for 75 questions (as of 2026-11).
questions.f: The AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Professional exam gives candidates 130 minutes for 65 questions (as of 2026-11).
questions.x: The Professional exam is longer than the associate-level format: 75 questions in 180 minutes, of which 65 are scored under the SAP-C02 guide. AWS kept the same length and duration for SAP-C03.

questions.t: AWS App Runner is no longer open to new customers, and AWS points new container web apps to Amazon ECS Express Mode instead.
questions.f: Amazon ECS Express Mode is no longer open to new customers, and AWS points new container web apps to AWS App Runner instead.
questions.x: App Runner gets no new features and is closed to new customers, though existing customers can keep creating services. ECS Express Mode is the suggested path, provisioning a Fargate service, an ALB and auto scaling from one API call.

questions.t: AWS cites savings of up to 90% with Spot Instances and up to 72% with Savings Plans compared with On-Demand pricing (as of 2026-11).
questions.f: AWS cites savings of up to 72% with Spot Instances and up to 90% with Savings Plans compared with On-Demand pricing (as of 2026-11).
questions.x: Spot offers the deepest discount because the capacity can be reclaimed. Savings Plans trade a usage commitment for a smaller maximum discount, so the false statement swaps the two figures.

questions.t: AWS Lambda's default concurrency quota is 1,000 executions per account per Region, and the quota can be adjusted.
questions.f: AWS Lambda's default concurrency quota is 1,000 executions per function per Region, and the quota can be adjusted.
questions.x: The 1,000-execution default is shared by all functions in an account within one Region. Treating it as a per-function allowance overstates how much concurrency an account has before requesting an increase.

questions.t: Each vCPU on an AWS Graviton instance is a full physical core rather than one hyperthread of a shared core.
questions.f: Each vCPU on an AWS Graviton instance is one hyperthread, with two vCPUs sharing every physical core.
questions.x: Graviton does not use simultaneous multithreading, so a vCPU maps to a whole core. AWS cites this as one reason for Graviton's efficiency.

questions.t: Graviton-based EC2 instances run Linux rather than Windows, so .NET Framework applications must be ported to modern .NET first.
questions.f: Graviton-based EC2 instances run Windows Server as well as Linux, so .NET Framework applications can move to them unchanged.
questions.x: Graviton EC2 targets Linux and BSD workloads that can be rebuilt for Arm64. Windows workloads, and .NET Framework code that has not been ported, are reasons to stay on x86.

questions.t: In an EC2 instance name such as M8gd, the g marks a Graviton processor and the d marks local NVMe storage.
questions.f: In an EC2 instance name such as M8gd, the g marks local NVMe storage and the d marks a Graviton processor.
questions.x: The letter g after the generation number signals Graviton, and an added d signals instance-attached NVMe disks, as in M9gd or C9gd.

questions.t: Amazon ECR basic scanning is provided and billed by ECR, while enhanced scanning is provided and billed by Amazon Inspector.
questions.f: Amazon ECR enhanced scanning is provided and billed by ECR, while basic scanning is provided and billed by Amazon Inspector.
questions.x: Basic scanning is ECR's own feature. Enhanced scanning hands the work to Amazon Inspector, which also covers programming-language packages and can rescan continuously when new CVEs appear.

questions.t: Pulling an ECR image to ECS, Fargate or Lambda in the same Region is free, while cross-Region pulls are charged at internet data transfer rates.
questions.f: Pulling an ECR image to ECS, Fargate or Lambda in another Region is free, while same-Region pulls are charged at internet data transfer rates.
questions.x: ECR charges nothing for inbound pushes or for same-Region pulls to AWS compute. Moving image data between Regions, by pulling or by replication, is billed like internet transfer.

questions.t: An ECR pull through cache rule mirrors images from an upstream registry such as Docker Hub into your private registry and re-checks the upstream for updates.
questions.f: An ECR replication rule mirrors images from an upstream registry such as Docker Hub into your private registry and re-checks the upstream for updates.
questions.x: Pull through cache is the feature for keeping copies of third-party images in ECR. Replication copies images you already hold in ECR to other Regions or accounts.

questions.t: EKS Auto Mode's built-in NodePools launch only On-Demand C, M and R instances, so Spot or GPU capacity needs a custom NodePool.
questions.f: EKS Auto Mode's built-in NodePools launch only Spot C, M and R instances, so On-Demand or GPU capacity needs a custom NodePool.
questions.x: The system and general-purpose pools are On-Demand only and limited to C, M and R families of generation 5 or newer, and they cannot be edited. Adding Spot or GPU instances means defining your own NodePool.
